title: 人工智能设计出具有生物活性的酶组分，这有助于拓展药物研发领域
content:
AI designs functional enzyme components that could help expand drug discovery
Lisa Lock
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
New active ingredients for drugs to treat infections, cancer or other serious diseases are often based on substances originally discovered in microorganisms, plants or other living organisms. Producing or improving such active ingredients in a targeted manner using microorganisms is often challenging because the underlying biological processes are extremely complex.
Researchers at the Helmholtz Institute for Pharmaceutical Research Saarland (HIPS) have now shown that artificial intelligence can help with this task. Using AI, they developed novel protein building blocks for biological production systems. The researchers published their findings in the journal Nature Communications.
The challenge of reprogramming natural producers
Nature offers a virtually limitless variety of chemical substances. Although these have been optimized over millions of years of evolution for their respective purposes, they have not been optimized for use as active ingredients in humans. For decades, researchers have therefore been attempting to genetically reprogram microbial producers of active ingredients so that they produce variants of their natural compounds with improved pharmaceutical properties.
A major challenge in this endeavor is that the protein structures responsible for the production of natural products are extremely complex. Many changes to the corresponding blueprints therefore simply result in nonfunctional proteins.
AI designs molecular transport arms
A team led by HIPS junior research group leader Dr. Kenan Bozhüyük has now addressed this problem with a new approach based on artificial intelligence. The idea is that if an AI can understand what makes production systems work, it may even be able to develop new building blocks for such systems that do not occur in nature—thereby further expanding chemical diversity for drug discovery.
The study focused on so-called non-ribosomal peptide synthetases, or NRPS for short. These large enzyme complexes function like molecular assembly lines. They produce a wide variety of biologically active natural compounds in microorganisms, including substances that have served as the basis for the development of numerous antibiotics, immunosuppressants and cancer drugs. The problem is that a product can only be formed if the individual components interact precisely at the right moment. This is why NRPS are particularly difficult to modify in a targeted manner.
The researchers combined several pretrained AI models with experimental test series to develop new so-called thiolation domains (T-domains). These building blocks act like movable transport arms within the NRPS: They pick up molecular intermediates and pass them on to the next processing station. In total, the team used AI to design 76 new T-domains, produced hundreds of different NRPS variants and tested them in living cells.
Higher yields from redesigned building blocks
The results showed that several of the AI-designed building blocks were functional. Some even enabled the formation of products in artificially combined enzyme systems and increased the yield up to three times compared to natural variants. In addition, at least one of the designed proteins proved to be more soluble and thermally more stable than the natural counterpart.
Higher yields are not only important for future production. They also make it easier, even in the early stages of research, to obtain new natural compounds in sufficient quantities to determine their structure and investigate their effects more closely. A key factor was that the AI did not design the new building blocks in isolation, but rather tailored them to their immediate surroundings within the respective enzyme system. This is because whether such a building block functions depends heavily on its ability to interact with its neighboring regions.
"Our results show that artificial intelligence can be used not only to design individual proteins, but also to specifically redesign key building blocks of complex biological production systems," says Bozhüyük. "AI does not replace experiments, but it helps us select promising candidates more quickly from among many possible variants."
"The study shows that AI can significantly advance the development of new active compounds based on natural products," says Rolf Müller, scientific director of HIPS and head of the Microbial Natural Products department. "If we can adapt such biosynthetic systems in a more targeted manner in the future, this will open up new possibilities for developing urgently needed drugs more efficiently and thus making them available for clinical applications more quickly."
Publication details
Emre F. Bülbül et al., Generative AI designs functional thiolation domains for reprogramming non-ribosomal peptide synthetases, Nature Communications (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77963-6
Journal information: Nature Communications

report.summary: AI设计出功能性酶组件，最高提产三倍
report.background: 许多抗生素、免疫抑制剂和抗癌药源自微生物天然产物。传统药物研发试图改造微生物的“生物合成流水线”，让它们生产药性更优的化合物，但负责合成的非核糖体肽合成酶（NRPS）是巨型多酶复合体，结构复杂，随意改动往往导致蛋白失活。HIPS团队因此尝试用AI理解并重设计其中的关键组件，以拓展天然产物的化学多样性。
key_points: 研究聚焦NRPS中的T结构域，它像分子“搬运臂”，负责抓取中间产物并传递到下一反应站。
团队把多个预训练AI模型与实验测试结合，设计76个全新T结构域，构建数百个NRPS变体并在活细胞中验证。
多个AI设计组件具备功能，部分使人工酶系统产量最高提升3倍；其中一个溶解性和热稳定性优于天然版本。
AI并非孤立设计蛋白，而是针对酶系统局部环境定制；AI负责缩小候选范围，实验仍是最终验证关键。
report.impact: 对AI行业而言，这显示生成式蛋白质设计正从单蛋白走向复杂多酶系统，打开“设计生物合成流水线”的新方向。对开发者，门槛在AI建模、合成生物学和高通量湿实验的闭环协作。对普通用户，短期不直接产生药物，但长期有望加快抗生素、抗癌药等急需药物的发现与量产。
report.tools: 可关注蛋白质生成与结构预测工具RFdiffusion、ProteinMPNN、ESM/AlphaFold、ColabFold，以及天然产物基因簇分析工具antiSMASH、MIBiG；上手路径是结构预测、定点设计加湿实验验证。
